Ongoing research and testing are essential in the development of air-breathing hypersonic propulsion technology.
Recent work was performed for GTX, a rocket-based combined-cycle, single-stage-to-orbit concept.
Structural optimization was applied to evaluate the feasibility of the GTX concept and determine the gross liftoff weight of the integrated system.
Achieving low Earth orbit with even a small payload requires an aggressive approach to weight minimization through the use of lightweight, oxidation-resistant composite materials.
NASA's APAS code was used to generate aerodynamic pressure and temperature profiles at each critical event.
Heat transfer solutions using NASA's MINIVER code and the SINDA code were calculated at selective points and then extrapolated over the entire exposed surface.
A detailed finite element model of the propulsion system was generated to establish a flight weight for one engine.
A second finite element model, more coarsely meshed, of the full integrated system was generated for the overall assessment, mapping of loads, and system optimization.
Loads were applied in a case-consistent fashion using MSC-NASTRAN for static analysis, with an inertia relief capability to simulate the vehicle in flight.
The weight of the structure was optimized using HyperSizer, which allows users to optimize a component structure according to the critical case for each component.
The methods used in this assessment were effective in defining and evaluating the integrated propulsion/vehicle structure.
The results of the analyses were used to improve scaling laws and increase the accuracy in the GTX sizing tool.
The research was conducted at the NASA Glenn Research Center.
The work was performed for the GTX, a rocket-based combined-cycle, single-stage-to-orbit concept.
The goal was to enable low Earth orbit with even a small payload.
